newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Trichet calls for fiscal rectitude.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Trichet calls for fiscal rectitude.

text.p: Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet warned the new Socialist government on Tuesday not to stray from the path of fiscal rectitude and said structural economic reform was vital to fighting record unemployment.

Sound monetary policy had brought interest rates to historic lows but was not enough to tackle France's 12.8 percent jobless rate, he told a news conference as he released the independent central bank's annual report.

Such action required structural reforms, sustained deficit reduction and controls on public spending, Trichet said, making the Bank's first major public statement since the Socialists ousted the centre-right in a parliamentary election on June 1.

"Structural reforms are imperative to increase employment," he said. Changes were needed in education, training and labour market flexibility, he said, and urged decision-makers to look beyond France's borders to seek ideas.
"We must be pragmatic and humble and look at what has worked elsewhere," he said, pointing to The Netherlands where the jobless rate is less than half that of France at 5.7 percent.
"The (monetary policy) council can only hope the government, parliament, trade unions and employers implement these reforms in a pragmatic, unbiased way."
He said the Bank's report had been written before Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's maiden address last week to parliament and was not intended as a response. But it was drafted after the election.

Jospin, who during the campaign urged a flexible reading of the Maastricht treaty goal of limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, told parliament the government was determined to launch the single currency on time. But he made no mention of meeting the deficit criteria strictly.
Trichet said he believed the euro would be started on time. But, in an apparent shift in emphasis, he also shied away from saying France would meet the three percent target strictly.
"I will favour implementation of the treaty as it is with the various decisions and diagnosis that have to be made," he told Reuters Financial Television.
Economists have said France could likely get away with a deficit of 3.5 percent of GDP but Germany would have enormous difficulty accepting France's participation if the deficit was over that amount.
Newspapers have said France's deficit to GDP ratio could be between 3.3 and 3.8 percent this year without new spending cuts.
Trichet's message on the need to keep cutting public deficits was "classic" and unsurprising but the timing was important given the change of government, economists said.

Trichet said total public spending at 54.7 percent of GDP was "clearly too high", noting the European Union average was 49.9 percent and the average was 39.7 percent in the Group of Seven leading industrial nations.

Jospin announced last Thursday a four percent rise in the national minimum wage from July 1 and said he would end the previous government's efforts to cut the public work force, a sign efforts to curb the budget deficit could face trouble.

But he calmed some market worries of profligacy by steering clear of pledging swift implementation of his most radical campaign policies, such as cutting the 39-hour work week to 35, and was ambiguous on the thorny issue of privatisations which he had pledged to halt.

Fielding questions, Trichet refused to be drawn on the new administration's policies. "We are not replying to the government's policy statement... But what we are saying ourselves is if one wants to create jobs, measures must be taken to reinforce competitiveness," he said.

At the same time, he noted in the daily Le Monde continued market confidence in France despite the government's "less European and less strict line on the goal of deficit reduction". He attributed this confidence to trust in the independent bank.

Trichet said France's 10-year interest rates were the third lowest in the world because the franc was stable and credible and promised the bank would continue its efforts to ensure the new euro inspired as much confidence as the franc.
